note: What this member claims about the audio unit, and where each claim came from. The unit has no published document, so almost everything here is either read off the part's own boot program or deferred to one of the two members this one is assembled from.

order: Nintendo's SNES Development Manual, Book I, for the control register and the timers, which it prints
the boot program, which is the part's own code and settles the console interface
checksums Shay Green took on a console, carried by checks this model now runs
the SNESdev wiki, for what those checksums settle without naming it
the two members this unit is assembled from, each with its own record
authority.why: Sony published no document for the S-SMP, and Nintendo did: Book I of its development manual prints the control register, the three timers and the prescaler that feeds them. That is the top rung and it is used wherever it speaks. Below it, the unit carries sixty four bytes of Sony's own code in its top page, so the console interface can be read off them rather than guessed at or copied. And Shay Green wrote checks that carry checksums he took on real hardware, which settle what neither of those touches. Those two are rung two, the artifact and a measurement of one, rather than agreement with another implementation.

comparedAgainst.what: Three of Shay Green's checks, run as they are, each carrying a checksum he took on a console. Beside them, and running separately in conformance/boot.test.py, the part's own boot program played the way a console plays it. Neither this repository nor either half of it wrote any of them.
comparedAgainst.why: Both are outside this unit. A check that drove the processor and the generator against each other would prove they agree, which they do just as perfectly when both are wrong.

authority.whatIsMissing: A Sony document. Nintendo's manual describes the unit for somebody programming it, so it prints the registers and the timer rates and says nothing about the memory bus, the clock between the processor and the generator, or what a reset leaves in memory.

developmentManual.title: SNES Development Manual, Book I
developmentManual.section: Section 3, Super NES Sound: chapter 1 Outline, chapter 4 Control Register, chapter 5 Timers
developmentManual.note: A scan with an OCR text layer. Pages 3-1-1 and 3-4-1 to 3-5-3, file pages 153 and 162 to 166, were read twice: off the text layer and off the page rendered at 150 dots per inch. The text layer prints T0 as TO and drops the figures, so the figure labels quoted here were read off the rendered page.

bootProgram.evidence: Read off the program itself and driven at the unit in conformance/boot.test.py. The clear loop stops when its index reaches zero, which is why the first byte survives.
bootProgram.howToSettleIt: Settled. The program is the part's own.

map.0xF0: test, written and never read; a read answers zero
map.0xF1: control: three timer enables, two port clears, and the boot window; a read answers zero
map.0xF8: spare 0, which reads back the last byte written to it whatever the memory beneath holds
map.0xF9: spare 1, which reads back the last byte written to it whatever the memory beneath holds
map.0xFA: timer 0 divider, written and never read; a read answers zero
map.0xFB: timer 1 divider, written and never read; a read answers zero
map.0xFC: timer 2 divider, written and never read; a read answers zero
map.0xFD: timer 0 counter, read and cleared by the read
map.0xFE: timer 1 counter, read and cleared by the read
map.0xFF: timer 2 counter, read and cleared by the read

registers.evidence: The boot program reaches 0xF1 through 0xF5, which confirms the control register, the boot window bit and the first two ports from the part's own code. All sixteen are settled at once by initial_regs.spc, which reads every one of them in order and compares a checksum of the result against a value taken on a console. Of every arrangement of the five that cannot be read, exactly one reproduces that checksum: all five answer zero. The SNESdev wiki says the same in words. The model answered with the memory underneath before this, and that check is what caught it.
registers.howToSettleIt: Settled. A Sony document would add a rung; nothing else would change the answer.
registers.writesReachMemory: Every write to the sixteen registers also lands in the memory beneath them, which the sound generator reads directly. Shay Green's spc_dsp6 check Misc/$F0-$FF are not ram reproduces its console value only with both this and the two spare registers holding what was written.

control.evidence: Book I draws the register in Figure 3-4-1 and Figure 3-4-3 with the three timer starts in bits 0 to 2 and the two port clears in bits 4 and 5, which is where this model has them. The boot window bit is drawn as unused there and is confirmed by the boot program instead, which runs out of the window and would not be reachable were the bit anywhere else.
control.howToSettleIt: Settled by the document for the five bits it draws and by the boot program for the sixth.

whenReset.meaning: A reset clears the three timer starts and the two port clears.

timers.evidence: Book I prints the prescaler's two rates, 8 kHz for timers 0 and 1 and 64 kHz for timer 2, and the shortest instruction time, 1.953 microseconds for an instruction the appendix gives as two cycles. A cycle is therefore 976.5 nanoseconds, and 125 and 15.6 microseconds are 128 and 16 of them. Shay Green's three random timer checks and his memory access check, taken on a console, agree with this model once the prescaler is shared and free running and the divider is matched by equality, as the manual draws and says.
timers.howToSettleIt: Settled by the document and by four checks taken on a console.

prescalerRates.quote: The clock input to timers T0 and T1 from the prescaler is 8KHz (125 µs) and the clock input to timer T2 from the prescaler is 64KHz (15.6 µs).
prescalerRates.section: Section 3, 5.1 Function of Timers T0, T1, and T2

instructionTime.quote: Minimum Command Execution Time : 1.953µs/2.48MHz when active
instructionTime.misprint: The clock beside the time reads 2.48 MHz on the rendered page and in the text layer. 1.953 microseconds is four periods of the 2.048 MHz clock Figure 3-5-1 prints, so the 2.48 is taken as a dropped zero and nothing here rests on it.

onePrescaler.meaning: One prescaler, on one 2.048 MHz clock, feeds all three timers. Switching a timer on clears that timer's own counters and leaves the prescaler running.

dividerMatch.quote: When its value corresponds to the contents of the timer register, it is cleared to 00H.
dividerMatch.meaning: The eight bit stage is compared for equality, so a divider lowered below the stage is reached only after the stage wraps through 255.

enableClears.quote: Count up commences when both upper and lower level counters are cleared by “1”.

readClears.quote: When the value of CN0 is read, only the 4-bit up counter section is cleared to “00”.

resetStops.quote: Action of timer T0 is stopped by means of the reset input (POR=”L”). At the time of reset, ST0 of the control register is “0” and; CN0 and TM0 of the timer register are indeterminate.

ports.evidence: Two bytes rather than one, one per direction. The boot program proves it: it writes 0xAA to port 0 and then compares port 0 against 0xCC, which can only both be true if a write from the unit and a read by the unit reach different bytes.
ports.howToSettleIt: Settled by the program that depends on it.

sets.generator: what resetLine in the sound generator's own record lists, applied by its reset()
sets.processor: what the processor's own record says its reset sets, with the program counter taken from the vector at 0xFFFE
sets.timerStarts: cleared, so all three timers stop, as Book I of Nintendo's development manual prints on page 3-5-2 and in Figure 3-4-3
sets.portClears: cleared, as Figure 3-4-1 prints, where a zero in those bits reads No Clear, so a reset clears no port

keeps: the four ports, in both directions
the three timers' dividers, stages and counters, which Book I calls indeterminate after a reset
control bits 3 and 6, which Figure 3-4-3 prints as dashes
reset.evidence: The boot window is settled by the boot program. It never writes 0xF1, and the processor leaves reset by reading its vector at 0xFFFE, which only the boot program supplies as 0xFFC0, so the window is visible whenever the processor comes out of reset. Book I prints the control register's reset value and that a reset stops timer 0, so the three timer starts clear. The generator and the processor are each held to their own records. Everything kept is kept because no source here says the reset line touches it, and the family standard leaves anything a reset does not define holding what it held.
reset.howToSettleIt: A capture of a real unit's registers and memory either side of a console reset, with the timers running and the ports written before it.

notStated: Any ratio between this unit's clock and the console's. They are separate crystals and neither divides the other, so no figure is published.

What the unit holds at power on, beyond what its two halves record for themselves. Book I prints no power-on value for any register, port, timer or the prescaler, so every one of them is scrambled from the seed at construction and none is cleared. Unverified: a capture of a real unit's registers at power on, repeated across power cycles, would settle it.

Control bits 3 and 6 at a reset. Figure 3-4-3 prints them as dashes, so a reset leaves them holding what they held. Unverified, and unobservable: the register reads zero and neither bit drives anything this model knows of.

Where the prescaler stands at a reset. Pages 3-4-1 to 3-5-3 of Book I name ST0, CN0 and TM0 at a reset and say nothing of the prescaler, so it keeps running from its power-on phase here. Unverified: a capture of the first timer tick after a console reset, against the reset edge, would settle it.

What the console's reset line sets in the ports, the test register and the sound generator's address register. Each is left holding what it held; see reset. The timer starts are printed and are cleared.
Whether memory survives a console reset on a real unit. It is kept here; see reset.

checksFromHardware.what: Checks by Shay Green, each carrying a value he took on a console.
checksFromHardware.found: One disagreement, since fixed: the five registers that cannot be read answered with the memory underneath rather than with zero.
checksFromHardware.shownToFail: The disagreement was reproduced on purpose after the fix, by putting the old behaviour back. initial_regs.spc disagreed on sub-check 3 and reported d57e2579 against the 9d4d2100 it wanted. The other two still agreed, because neither reads those registers.
checksFromHardware.evidence: The checksums are the author's, taken on hardware, and are not this project's.
checksFromHardware.howToSettleIt: Settled for what these three cover.

generator.why: Voices read their compressed blocks out of the same sixty four kilobytes the processor runs on and the echo unit writes back into it, so the two halves share one store. The clock is one for one: the crystal reaches the processor through a divisor of 24 and the generator through 768 for a sample with 32 clocks inside it, and 24 times 32 is 768. A unit is built as the rail coming up leaves it, with the generator and the processor both scrambled, and the unit's reset() is the console's reset line, which reaches both: it resets the generator to what its own record's resetLine lists and the processor to its reset vector. What a scrambled generator writes before that reset is modelled rather than prevented.
generator.evidence: Shay Green's spc_dsp6.sfc, run through this unit, reaches 104 verdicts and all 104 agree with values he took on a console. Its 41 timing checks read and write the generator's registers at named steps of the thirty two step schedule, timed by the processor's own instructions, so they hold the one-clock-per-cycle wiring. The crystal arithmetic in ssmp/rates.py is the reasoning behind it.
generator.howToSettleIt: The wiring is settled by the timing group of spc_dsp6.sfc. What the generator produces is not this member's claim: it is held in sony-s-dsp-python's own record, and a recording of a real unit playing a known program would settle it.
